tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: propose it and call this.

The result says which case below applies. When the box shows your question, it ends your turn: write no text after this call, since the recap and question say what the user needs and your work above holds the detail. Otherwise your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, with any question the box did not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

# `screenings.csv` — data dictionary

Synthetic export. One row per customer whose **first** screening took place in 2025.
Export date: **30.09.2026**. Second screenings are only visible up to that date.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `customer_id` | Pseudonymous customer ID |
| `location_id` | Where the first screening took place |
| `location_type` | `optician_chain`, `independent_optician` or `mobile_unit` (a screening bus visiting companies and town squares) |
| `city` | City of the location |
| `optician_follow_up` | What the location does after a screening on its own initiative: `none`, `email`, `phone`. Self-reported by the optician in a partner survey |
| `first_screening_date` | Date of the first screening (YYYY-MM-DD) |
| `age_band` | `18-39`, `40-59`, `60+` |
| `preferred_language` | Language chosen at booking (`de`, `en`, `tr`, `ru`, `ar`, `pl`). The report is currently German only |
| `result_category` | Ophthalmologist's evaluation: `unremarkable`, `minor_findings` (no referral, but worth watching), `referral_recommended` |
| `report_opened` | Whether the customer opened the result report at least once |
| `report_opened_days_after` | Days between report available and first open; empty if never opened |
| `marketing_consent` | Whether the customer agreed at booking to be contacted for reminders and offers |
| `referral_booked` | Only for `referral_recommended`: whether an appointment at a partner practice was booked. Empty otherwise |
| `second_screening_date` | Date of the next screening at any mira location; empty if none yet |

# Synthesize Research

> If you see unfamiliar placeholders or need to check which tools are connected, see [CONNECTORS.md](../../CONNECTORS.md).

Synthesize user research from multiple sources into structured insights and recommendations.

## Usage

```
/synthesize-research Workflow step 2: synthesize data/interviews/, data/optician-survey.md, data/customer-journey.md, data/constraints.md, output/01-cohort.md into output/02-synthesis.md with only sections: constraints, journey drop-off, themes with two sources, contradictions, at most two candidate flows. No personas, no recommendations.
```

## Workflow

### 1. Gather Research Inputs

Accept research from any combination of:
- **Pasted text**: Interview notes, transcripts, survey responses, feedback
- **Uploaded files**: Research documents, spreadsheets, recordings summaries
- **~~knowledge base** (if connected): Search for research documents, interview notes, survey results
- **~~user feedback** (if connected): Pull recent support tickets, feature requests, bug reports
- **~~product analytics** (if connected): Pull usage data, funnel metrics, behavioral data
- **~~meeting transcription** (if connected): Pull interview recordings, meeting summaries, and discussion notes

Ask the user what they have:
- What type of research? (interviews, surveys, usability tests, analytics, support tickets, sales call notes)
- How many sources / participants?
- Is there a specific question or hypothesis they are investigating?
- What decisions will this research inform?

### 2. Process the Research

For each source, extract:
- **Key observations**: What did users say, do, or experience?
- **Quotes**: Verbatim quotes that illustrate important points
- **Behaviors**: What users actually did (vs what they said they do)
- **Pain points**: Frustrations, workarounds, and unmet needs
- **Positive signals**: What works well, moments of delight
- **Context**: User segment, use case, experience level

### 3. Identify Themes and Patterns

Apply thematic analysis — see **Research Synthesis Methodology** below for detailed guidance on thematic analysis, affinity mapping, and triangulation techniques.

Group observations into themes, count frequency across participants, and assess impact severity. Note contradictions and surprises.

Create a priority matrix:
- **High frequency + High impact**: Top priority findings
- **Low frequency + High impact**: Important for specific segments
- **High frequency + Low impact**: Quality-of-life improvements
- **Low frequency + Low impact**: Note but deprioritize

### 4. Generate the Synthesis

Produce a structured research synthesis:

#### Research Overview
- Methodology: what types of research, how many participants/sources
- Research question(s): what we set out to learn
- Timeframe: when the research was conducted

#### Key Findings
For each major finding (aim for 5-8):
- **Finding statement**: One clear sentence describing the insight
- **Evidence**: Supporting quotes, data points, or observations (with source attribution)
- **Frequency**: How many participants/sources support this finding
- **Impact**: How significantly this affects the user experience or business
- **Confidence level**: High (strong evidence), Medium (suggestive), Low (early signal)

Order findings by priority (frequency x impact).

#### User Segments / Personas
If the research reveals distinct user segments:
- Segment name and description
- Key characteristics and behaviors
- Unique needs and pain points
- Size estimate if data is available

#### Opportunity Areas
Based on the findings, identify opportunity areas:
- What user needs are unmet or underserved
- Where do current solutions fall short
- What new capabilities would unlock value
- Prioritized by potential impact

#### Recommendations
Specific, actionable recommendations:
- What to build, change, or investigate further
- Tied back to specific findings
- Prioritized by impact and feasibility

#### Open Questions
What the research did not answer:
- Gaps in understanding
- Areas needing further investigation
- Suggested follow-up research methods

### 5. Review and Extend

After generating the synthesis:
- Ask if any findings need more detail or different framing
- Offer to generate specific artifacts: persona documents, opportunity maps, research presentations
- Offer to create follow-up research plans for open questions
- Offer to draft product implications (how findings should influence the roadmap)

## Research Synthesis Methodology

### Thematic Analysis
The core method for synthesizing qualitative research:

1. **Familiarization**: Read through all the data. Get a feel for the overall landscape before coding anything.
2. **Initial coding**: Go through the data systematically. Tag each observation, quote, or data point with descriptive codes. Be generous with codes — it is easier to merge than to split later.
3. **Theme development**: Group related codes into candidate themes. A theme captures something important about the data in relation to the research question.
4. **Theme review**: Check themes against the data. Does each theme have sufficient evidence? Are themes distinct from each other? Do they tell a coherent story?
5. **Theme refinement**: Define and name each theme clearly. Write a 1-2 sentence description of what each theme captures.
6. **Report**: Write up the themes as findings with supporting evidence.

### Affinity Mapping
A collaborative method for grouping observations:

1. **Capture observations**: Write each distinct observation, quote, or data point as a separate note
2. **Cluster**: Group related notes together based on similarity. Do not pre-define categories — let them emerge from the data.
3. **Label clusters**: Give each cluster a descriptive name that captures the common thread
4. **Organize clusters**: Arrange clusters into higher-level groups if patterns emerge
5. **Identify themes**: The clusters and their relationships reveal the key themes

**Tips for affinity mapping**:
- One observation per note. Do not combine multiple insights.
- Move notes between clusters freely. The first grouping is rarely the best.
- If a cluster gets too large, it probably contains multiple themes. Split it.
- Outliers are interesting. Do not force every observation into a cluster.
- The process of grouping is as valuable as the output. It builds shared understanding.

### Triangulation
Strengthen findings by combining multiple data sources:

- **Methodological triangulation**: Same question, different methods (interviews + survey + analytics)
- **Source triangulation**: Same method, different participants or segments
- **Temporal triangulation**: Same observation at different points in time

A finding supported by multiple sources and methods is much stronger than one supported by a single source. When sources disagree, that is interesting — it may reveal different user segments or contexts.

## Interview Note Analysis

### Extracting Insights from Interview Notes
For each interview, identify:

**Observations**: What did the participant describe doing, experiencing, or feeling?
- Distinguish between behaviors (what they do) and attitudes (what they think/feel)
- Note context: when, where, with whom, how often
- Flag workarounds — these are unmet needs in disguise

**Direct quotes**: Verbatim statements that powerfully illustrate a point
- Good quotes are specific and vivid, not generic
- Attribute to participant type, not name: "Enterprise admin, 200-person team" not "Sarah"
- A quote is evidence, not a finding. The finding is your interpretation of what the quote means.

**Behaviors vs stated preferences**: What people DO often differs from what they SAY they want
- Behavioral observations are stronger evidence than stated preferences
- If a participant says "I want feature X" but their workflow shows they never use similar features, note the contradiction
- Look for revealed preferences through actual behavior

**Signals of intensity**: How much does this matter to the participant?
- Emotional language: frustration, excitement, resignation
- Frequency: how often do they encounter this issue
- Workarounds: how much effort do they expend working around the problem
- Impact: what is the consequence when things go wrong

### Cross-Interview Analysis
After processing individual interviews:
- Look for patterns: which observations appear across multiple participants?
- Note frequency: how many participants mentioned each theme?
- Identify segments: do different types of users have different patterns?
- Surface contradictions: where do participants disagree? This often reveals meaningful segments.
- Find surprises: what challenged your prior assumptions?

## Survey Data Interpretation

### Quantitative Survey Analysis
- **Response rate**: How representative is the sample? Low response rates may introduce bias.
- **Distribution**: Look at the shape of responses, not just averages. A bimodal distribution (lots of 1s and 5s) tells a different story than a normal distribution (lots of 3s).
- **Segmentation**: Break down responses by user segment. Aggregates can mask important differences.
- **Statistical significance**: For small samples, be cautious about drawing conclusions from small differences.
- **Benchmark comparison**: How do scores compare to industry benchmarks or previous surveys?

### Open-Ended Survey Response Analysis
- Treat open-ended responses like mini interview notes
- Code each response with themes
- Count frequency of themes across responses
- Pull representative quotes for each theme
- Look for themes that appear in open-ended responses but not in structured questions — these are things you did not think to ask about

### Common Survey Analysis Mistakes
- Reporting averages without distributions. A 3.5 average could mean everyone is lukewarm or half love it and half hate it.
- Ignoring non-response bias. The people who did not respond may be systematically different.
- Over-interpreting small differences. A 0.1 point change in NPS is noise, not signal.
- Treating Likert scales as interval data. The difference between "Strongly Agree" and "Agree" is not necessarily the same as between "Agree" and "Neutral."
- Confusing correlation with causation in cross-tabulations.

## Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Insights

### The Qual-Quant Feedback Loop
- **Qualitative first**: Interviews and observation reveal WHAT is happening and WHY. They generate hypotheses.
- **Quantitative validation**: Surveys and analytics reveal HOW MUCH and HOW MANY. They test hypotheses at scale.
- **Qualitative deep-dive**: Return to qualitative methods to understand unexpected quantitative findings.

### Integration Strategies
- Use quantitative data to prioritize qualitative findings. A theme from interviews is more important if usage data shows it affects many users.
- Use qualitative data to explain quantitative anomalies. A drop in retention is a number; interviews reveal it is because of a confusing onboarding change.
- Present combined evidence: "47% of surveyed users report difficulty with X (survey), and interviews reveal this is because Y (qualitative finding)."

### When Sources Disagree
- Quantitative and qualitative sources may tell different stories. This is signal, not error.
- Check if the disagreement is due to different populations being measured
- Check if stated preferences (survey) differ from actual behavior (analytics)
- Check if the quantitative question captured what you think it captured
- Report the disagreement honestly and investigate further rather than choosing one source

## Persona Development from Research

### Building Evidence-Based Personas
Personas should emerge from research data, not imagination:

1. **Identify behavioral patterns**: Look for clusters of similar behaviors, goals, and contexts across participants
2. **Define distinguishing variables**: What dimensions differentiate one cluster from another? (e.g., company size, technical skill, usage frequency, primary use case)
3. **Create persona profiles**: For each behavioral cluster:
   - Name and brief description
   - Key behaviors and goals
   - Pain points and needs
   - Context (role, company, tools used)
   - Representative quotes
4. **Validate with data**: Can you size each persona segment using quantitative data?

### Persona Template
```
[Persona Name] — [One-line description]

Who they are:
- Role, company type/size, experience level
- How they found/started using the product

What they are trying to accomplish:
- Primary goals and jobs to be done
- How they measure success

How they use the product:
- Frequency and depth of usage
- Key workflows and features used
- Tools they use alongside this product

Key pain points:
- Top 3 frustrations or unmet needs
- Workarounds they have developed

What they value:
- What matters most in a solution
- What would make them switch or churn

Representative quotes:
- 2-3 verbatim quotes that capture this persona's perspective
```

### Common Persona Mistakes
- Demographic personas: defining by age/gender/location instead of behavior. Behavior predicts product needs better than demographics.
- Too many personas: 3-5 is the sweet spot. More than that and they are not actionable.
- Fictional personas: made up based on assumptions rather than research data.
- Static personas: never updated as the product and market evolve.
- Personas without implications: a persona that does not change any product decisions is not useful.

## Opportunity Sizing

### Estimating Opportunity Size
For each research finding or opportunity area, estimate:

- **Addressable users**: How many users could benefit from addressing this? Use product analytics, survey data, or market data to estimate.
- **Frequency**: How often do affected users encounter this issue? (Daily, weekly, monthly, one-time)
- **Severity**: How much does this issue impact users when it occurs? (Blocker, significant friction, minor annoyance)
- **Willingness to pay**: Would addressing this drive upgrades, retention, or new customer acquisition?

### Opportunity Scoring
Score opportunities on a simple matrix:

- **Impact**: (Users affected) x (Frequency) x (Severity) = impact score
- **Evidence strength**: How confident are we in the finding? (Multiple sources > single source, behavioral data > stated preferences)
- **Strategic alignment**: Does this opportunity align with company strategy and product vision?
- **Feasibility**: Can we realistically address this? (Technical feasibility, resource availability, time to impact)

### Presenting Opportunity Sizing
- Be transparent about assumptions and confidence levels
- Show the math: "Based on support ticket volume, approximately 2,000 users per month encounter this issue. Interview data suggests 60% of them consider it a significant blocker."
- Use ranges rather than false precision: "This affects 1,500-2,500 users monthly" not "This affects 2,137 users monthly"
- Compare opportunities against each other to create a relative ranking, not just absolute scores

## Output Format

Use clear headers and structured formatting. Each finding should stand on its own — a reader should be able to read any single finding and understand it without reading the rest.

## Tips

- Let the data speak. Do not force findings into a predetermined narrative.
- Distinguish between what users say and what they do. Behavioral data is stronger than stated preferences.
- Quotes are powerful evidence. Include them generously, with attribution to participant type (not name).
- Be explicit about confidence levels. A finding from 2 interviews is a hypothesis, not a conclusion.
- Contradictions in the data are interesting, not inconvenient. They often reveal distinct user segments.
- Recommendations should be specific enough to act on. "Improve onboarding" is not actionable. "Add a progress indicator to the setup flow" is.
- Resist the temptation to synthesize too many themes. 5-8 strong findings are better than 20 weak ones.

=== data/customer-journey.md
# The customer journey today

Simplified for this case. Some details differ from the live product.

## 1. Booking

- The customer books online (on the optician's website or our booking page) or at the store
  counter. Most bookings at independent opticians happen at the counter.
- Online booking asks for name, e-mail, date of birth, preferred language, and two checkboxes:
  terms (required) and "I'd like reminders and offers" (optional, unticked by default).
- **E-mail 1 — booking confirmation:** date, time, address, what to expect, "please don't wear
  contact lenses on the day".
- **E-mail 2 — reminder:** 24 hours before the appointment.

## 2. Screening at the optician (15 min)

- An examiner (usually optician staff trained by us) runs the screening on the mira devices:
  vision test, lens assessment, retinal images, eye-pressure measurement, slit-lamp photos.
- At the end the examiner says the results will arrive by e-mail within 48 hours. Some opticians
  use the moment to show frames or contact lenses; most don't.
- The customer pays 69 € at the counter.

## 3. Evaluation and report

- An ophthalmologist evaluates the images remotely within 48 hours.
- **E-mail 3 — "Your result is ready":** a link to log in and download the report (PDF). The
  e-mail itself contains no result.
- The report is 4 pages, in German: images, measured values, the ophthalmologist's assessment in
  medical language, and — if relevant — a recommendation to see an ophthalmologist.
- The report has **no** recommendation for when to come back for the next screening.

## 4. After the report

- If a referral is recommended, the report lists partner practices nearby. The customer books
  there themselves.
- If the result is unremarkable or has minor findings: **no further contact** from Mirantus.
- Whether the optician gets in touch depends entirely on the optician (see
  `optician_follow_up` in the CSV).

=== data/interviews/01-customer-leipzig.md
# Interview 1 — Customer, 67, Leipzig

Synthetic. Notes taken by a researcher during a 30-min phone call, partly verbatim. Interview in German.

- Screened in March 2025 at an independent optician she's been going to "seit über 20 Jahren".
- Came because the optician mentioned it while she picked up new glasses. "Herr K. hat gesagt,
  das sollte man in meinem Alter mal machen. Dann hab ich's halt gemacht."
- Result: unremarkable.
- Got the e-mail, opened the PDF "kurz". "Da standen lauter Fachbegriffe drin. Ich hab nur
  geguckt, ob irgendwo was Rotes steht. Stand nichts, also war alles gut."
- Asked whether she'd go again: "Warum? War doch alles in Ordnung." Then, after a pause: "Wenn
  Herr K. sagt, ich soll wieder kommen, dann komm ich wieder."
- Doesn't remember the name Mirantus or mira. Calls it "der Augen-Check bei Herrn K.".
- Doesn't use apps for health things. Uses WhatsApp with her grandchildren. Reads e-mail "ab und
  zu".
- Her sister has glaucoma ("Grüner Star"). She didn't mention this at the screening; nobody asked.
- Paid 69 € — "für einmal okay, aber jedes Jahr? Weiß ich nicht."
=== data/interviews/02-customer-berlin.md
# Interview 2 — Customer, 44, Berlin

Synthetic. Notes from a 30-min video call, in English.

- Software developer, moved to Berlin from Lisbon 6 years ago. German "okay for shopping, not for
  doctors".
- Booked online after seeing a poster in a chain optician's window. "I liked that I didn't need a
  doctor's appointment. Getting one at an ophthalmologist here takes months."
- Result: referral recommended (eye pressure slightly high).
- The report was in German. Used Google Translate on the PDF; "half of it made no sense". Wasn't
  sure how urgent the referral was.
- Booked a partner practice from the list; earliest slot was 6 weeks out. Went; was told to come
  back in a year for another pressure check.
- "Honestly I'd love a reminder. Just WhatsApp me in a year. I will forget otherwise."
- Then: "But not from the optician. I don't even remember which store it was. I'd want it from
  whoever has my results."
- Would pay again; would like the report "in English and in normal words".
- Ticked the reminders box at booking. Has received nothing since the report.
=== data/interviews/03-optician-bavaria.md
# Interview 3 — Optician, owner of 2 independent stores, Bavaria

Synthetic. Notes from a 45-min visit in her store, in German, translated by the interviewer where
marked.

- Runs mira in both stores since 2024. Around 30 screenings a month across both.
- Why she offers it: "Die Leute kommen rein, und manche kaufen danach eine Brille. Und es
  unterscheidet uns von der Kette nebenan."
- On reminders: [translated] "The customers are mine. If someone writes to them, it's me. I don't
  want them getting e-mails from a company they've never heard of."
- Her staff call customers when glasses are ready for pickup. She says they could "theoretically"
  call screening customers after a year, "aber wer soll sich das merken?" She has a CRM from her
  cash-register vendor; doesn't know if it can do reminders.
- Staff turnover is high; the trained examiner in store 2 left in summer, screenings there dropped
  to almost zero for 6 weeks.
- Thinks customers don't want to be bothered: [translated] "Older customers find it pushy if you
  call them for something they didn't ask for."
- When asked about her own data: knows that "a few" customers came back, can't say how many.
- Wish: "A list. Who should come back this month. Then my people can call."
=== data/interviews/04-ophthalmologist.md
# Interview 4 — Ophthalmologist, evaluating partner

Synthetic. Notes from a 30-min call, in German, translated by the interviewer.

- Evaluates around 200 mira screenings a month, remotely, in the evenings.
- On intervals (general guidance, "depends on the person"): under 40 without risk factors every
  2–3 years; 40 and over every 1–2 years; family history of glaucoma, diabetes or high myopia —
  yearly.
- "An unremarkable result is a snapshot, not a guarantee. Patients read it as 'I'm healthy'."
- The evaluation form she fills in has no field for a recommended interval. "I would fill it in
  if it were there. It takes five seconds."
- Risk factors like family history aren't asked at the screening, so she often can't tell who
  should come back sooner.
- Warns against fear: "If you scare people, the ones who come are the anxious ones, not the ones
  at risk."
- On referrals: [translated] "The referral customers I worry about less — they're in the medical
  system now. It's the 'unremarkable' 60-year-olds who disappear."
- Reports: "They are written for colleagues, honestly. Not for patients."
=== output/01-cohort.md
# 01 — Return cohort

Source: `data/screenings.csv` (synthetic, 9,000 rows, one per customer, first screening 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-28). Export date 2026-09-30. Only columns defined in `data/README.md` are used. All numbers come from `scratchpad/cohort.py`.

## 1. Metric

**Second-screening return rate** = customers with a non-empty `second_screening_date` / customers in the cohort.

| | Numerator (returned) | Denominator | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Naive, all customers | 304 | 9,000 | 3.4% |
| **Eligible cohort (headline)** | **287** | **5,773** | **5.0%** |

The naive rate counts customers who have not had a full year yet as "not returned", so it understates the return rate by 1.6 pp.

Time to return (from first to second screening, returners only): median **380 days** across all 304 returners (IQR 330–426, range 199–581). For the 287 eligible returners the median is 385 days. No second screening falls on or before the first screening date, and none falls after the export date.

## 2. Not yet eligible

- Eligible means `first_screening_date` ≤ 2025-09-30, so the customer has had at least 12 months to return. That gives **5,773 customers** (Jan to Sep 2025).
- **Not yet eligible:** 3,227 customers with a first screening from 2025-10-01 to 2025-12-28. They are **not counted as not returned**.
- **17 of these 3,227 have already returned** (208–345 days after the first screening). They are kept out of the headline rate.
- Eligible-cohort rate: **287 / 5,773 = 5.0%**.

Caveat: eligible customers do not all have the same amount of time. A January customer has had about 21 months and a September customer exactly 12. Because the median return comes after 380 days, longer follow-up mechanically raises the rate. As a check on equal footing, the rate for returning **within 365 days** of the first screening is 114 / 5,773 = **2.0%**.

## 3. Cuts (eligible cohort, n = 5,773)

Gap = percentage points against the best segment in the cut. Rows are sorted from the largest gap down. "Short" = n × gap, which is roughly how many more returns the segment would have at the best segment's rate. Segments with n < 100 are flagged *small*.

### result_category
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| unremarkable | 3,995 | 140 | 3.5% | −6.6 | 265 |
| referral_recommended | 564 | 24 | 4.3% | −5.9 | 33 |
| minor_findings | 1,214 | 123 | 10.1% | best | – |

### age_band
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 18-39 | 1,313 | 36 | 2.7% | −3.9 | 51 |
| 40-59 | 2,414 | 116 | 4.8% | −1.8 | 43 |
| 60+ | 2,046 | 135 | 6.6% | best | – |

### location_type
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mobile_unit | 302 | 3 | 1.0% | −4.9 | 15 |
| optician_chain | 2,360 | 100 | 4.2% | −1.7 | 40 |
| independent_optician | 3,111 | 184 | 5.9% | best | – |

### city
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Freiburg | 412 | 13 | 3.2% | −4.3 | 18 |
| Hannover | 514 | 18 | 3.5% | −4.0 | 21 |
| Leipzig | 328 | 12 | 3.7% | −3.8 | 13 |
| Stuttgart | 394 | 15 | 3.8% | −3.7 | 15 |
| Köln | 653 | 26 | 4.0% | −3.5 | 23 |

| Bremen | 374 | 17 | 4.5% | −3.0 | 11 |
| Kassel | 163 | 8 | 4.9% | −2.6 | 4 |
| Dresden | 304 | 17 | 5.6% | −1.9 | 6 |
| Regensburg | 250 | 14 | 5.6% | −1.9 | 5 |
| Hamburg | 244 | 14 | 5.7% | −1.8 | 4 |

| Berlin | 200 | 15 | 7.5% | best | – |

The city counts are small (8 to 35 returns each), so most of these differences are within noise. City also overlaps with location_type and follow-up, which this cut does not separate.

### optician_follow_up (self-reported by the optician)
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | 3,192 | 132 | 4.1% | −4.1 | 131 |
| email | 1,854 | 95 | 5.1% | −3.1 | 58 |
| phone | 727 | 60 | 8.3% | best | – |

### Month of first_screening_date
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short | Returned ≤365 d | Rate ≤365 d |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-06 | 702 | 24 | 3.4% | −3.9 | 27 | 12 | 1.7% |
| 2025-09 | 877 | 30 | 3.4% | −3.9 | 34 | 27 | 3.1% |
| 2025-08 | 713 | 28 | 3.9% | −3.4 | 24 | 13 | 1.8% |

| 2025-02 | 498 | 34 | 6.8% | −0.5 | 2 | 13 | 2.6% |

The gap by month mostly reflects how long each month has been observed. With a fixed 365-day window the ordering does not hold (September becomes the highest month). **This is not a leak.**

### preferred_language (the README says the report is German only)
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| en | 344 | 11 | 3.2% | −2.0 | 7 |
| pl | 118 | 4 | 3.4% | −1.8 | 2 |
| ru | 170 | 6 | 3.5% | −1.7 | 3 |
| ar | 114 | 5 | 4.4% | −0.8 | 1 |

| *(all non-de)* | 1,054 | 40 | 3.8% | −1.4 | 15 |

Report open rate: de 71.7%, non-de 37.3%.

### report_opened
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| false | 1,995 | 44 | 2.2% | −4.2 | 84 |
| true | 3,778 | 243 | 6.4% | best | – |

### marketing_consent
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| false | 2,611 | 96 | 3.7% | −2.4 | 62 |
| true | 3,162 | 191 | 6.0% | best | – |

### referral_booked (within result_category = referral_recommended, n = 564)
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| false | 277 | 10 | 3.6% | −1.3 | 4 |
| true | 287 | 14 | 4.9% | best | – |

### Two-way: preferred_language × report_opened
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| de / not opened | 1,334 | 28 | 2.1% | −4.4 |
| non-de / not opened | 661 | 16 | 2.4% | −4.0 |
| non-de / opened | 393 | 24 | 6.1% | −0.4 |
| de / opened | 3,385 | 219 | 6.5% | best |

Once you hold `report_opened` fixed, the language gap almost disappears (0.4 pp among openers, and reversed among non-openers). Non-German customers return less mainly because fewer of them open the report.

### Two-way: result_category × optician_follow_up (the two largest-volume gaps)
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| referral_recommended / none | 312 | 8 | 2.6% | −15.8 | 49 |
| unremarkable / none | 2,182 | 69 | 3.2% | −15.2 | 332 |
| unremarkable / email | 1,322 | 48 | 3.6% | −14.7 | 195 |
| referral_recommended / email | 163 | 6 | 3.7% | −14.7 | 24 |
| unremarkable / phone | 491 | 23 | 4.7% | −13.7 | 67 |
| minor_findings / none | 698 | 55 | 7.9% | −10.5 | 73 |
| minor_findings / email | 369 | 41 | 11.1% | −7.3 | 27 |
| referral_recommended / phone | 89 | 10 | 11.2% | −7.1 | 6 *(small)* |
| minor_findings / phone | 147 | 27 | 18.4% | best | – |

Neither gap explains the other. The result gap holds at every follow-up level, and the follow-up gap holds within every result. The result gap also holds when report_opened is held fixed: openers are at 4.3% for unremarkable vs 13.9% for minor_findings, and non-openers at 2.0% vs 3.3%. It also holds within every age band.

## 4. Main leak

The largest gap that is big enough to matter is among customers with an **`unremarkable`** result. They make up 3,995 of the 5,773 eligible customers (69%) and return at 3.5%, against 10.1% for **`minor_findings`**, the comparator. That is a 6.6 pp gap, about 265 returns short, and it persists within every follow-up type, age band and report-opened group.

# Interview 4 — Ophthalmologist, evaluating partner

Synthetic. Notes from a 30-min call, in German, translated by the interviewer.

- Evaluates around 200 mira screenings a month, remotely, in the evenings.
- On intervals (general guidance, "depends on the person"): under 40 without risk factors every
  2–3 years; 40 and over every 1–2 years; family history of glaucoma, diabetes or high myopia —
  yearly.

# 01 — Return cohort

Source: `data/screenings.csv` (synthetic, 9,000 rows, one per customer, first screening 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-28). Export date 2026-09-30. Only columns defined in `data/README.md` are used. All numbers come from `scratchpad/cohort.py`.

## 1. Metric

**Second-screening return rate** = customers with a non-empty `second_screening_date` / customers in the cohort.

| | Numerator (returned) | Denominator | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Naive, all customers | 304 | 9,000 | 3.4% |
| **Eligible cohort (headline)** | **287** | **5,773** | **5.0%** |

The naive rate counts customers who have not had a full year yet as "not returned", so it understates the return rate by 1.6 pp.

Time to return (from first to second screening, returners only): median **380 days** across all 304 returners (IQR 330–426, range 199–581). For the 287 eligible returners the median is 385 days. No second screening falls on or before the first screening date, and none falls after the export date.

## 2. Not yet eligible

- Eligible means `first_screening_date` ≤ 2025-09-30, so the customer has had at least 12 months to return. That gives **5,773 customers** (Jan to Sep 2025).
- **Not yet eligible:** 3,227 customers with a first screening from 2025-10-01 to 2025-12-28. They are **not counted as not returned**.
- **17 of these 3,227 have already returned** (208–345 days after the first screening). They are kept out of the headline rate.
- Eligible-cohort rate: **287 / 5,773 = 5.0%**.

Caveat: eligible customers do not all have the same amount of time. A January customer has had about 21 months and a September customer exactly 12. Because the median return comes after 380 days, longer follow-up mechanically raises the rate. As a check on equal footing, the rate for returning **within 365 days** of the first screening is 114 / 5,773 = **2.0%**.

Gap = percentage points against the best segment in the cut. Rows are sorted from the largest gap down. "Short" = n × gap, which is roughly how many more returns the segment would have at the best segment's rate. Segments with n < 100 are flagged *small*.

Once you hold `report_opened` fixed, the language gap almost disappears (0.4 pp among openers, and reversed among non-openers). Non-German customers return less mainly because fewer of them open the report.

### Two-way: result_category × optician_follow_up (the two largest-volume gaps)
| Segment | n | Returned | Rate | Gap (pp) | Short |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| referral_recommended / none | 312 | 8 | 2.6% | −15.8 | 49 |
| unremarkable / none | 2,182 | 69 | 3.2% | −15.2 | 332 |
| unremarkable / email | 1,322 | 48 | 3.6% | −14.7 | 195 |
| referral_recommended / email | 163 | 6 | 3.7% | −14.7 | 24 |
| unremarkable / phone | 491 | 23 | 4.7% | −13.7 | 67 |
| minor_findings / none | 698 | 55 | 7.9% | −10.5 | 73 |
| minor_findings / email | 369 | 41 | 11.1% | −7.3 | 27 |

| minor_findings / phone | 147 | 27 | 18.4% | best | – |

Neither gap explains the other. The result gap holds at every follow-up level, and the follow-up gap holds within every result. The result gap also holds when report_opened is held fixed: openers are at 4.3% for unremarkable vs 13.9% for minor_findings, and non-openers at 2.0% vs 3.3%. It also holds within every age band.

## 4. Main leak

The largest gap that is big enough to matter is among customers with an **`unremarkable`** result. They make up 3,995 of the 5,773 eligible customers (69%) and return at 3.5%, against 10.1% for **`minor_findings`**, the comparator. # 02 — Synthesis

Sources: 4 interviews (`data/interviews/01`–`04`), 15 optician survey answers (`data/optician-survey.md`, cited as S1–S15), `data/customer-journey.md`, `data/constraints.md`, `output/01-cohort.md`. All data is synthetic. Numbers come only from `output/01-cohort.md`. No personas, no recommendation.

## 1. Constraints (from `data/constraints.md`, quoted)

- Consent: "Customers may only receive reminders or marketing if they gave `marketing_consent` at booking." Without it, only messages "needed to deliver the service already bought". Consent "can be asked for again later, but only in a message the customer already receives legitimately, or in person."
- Medical: "Recommending a screening interval to a specific customer counts as a medical statement: it must come from the ophthalmologist's evaluation, not from marketing copy." "No fear-based messaging."
- Relationship: "Mirantus may contact customers only for the service itself, or on the optician's behalf and with the optician's name on it." "Opticians can't be required to do extra work, but they can be offered tools."
- Capacity: "One squad for one quarter: 2 engineers, 1 designer, you." "The report PDF and e-mails can be changed. The opticians' own systems (their CRMs, cash registers) can't be integrated this quarter."

## 2. Journey drop-off

The main leak from step 1: `unremarkable` customers, 3,995 of 5,773 eligible (69%), return at 3.5% vs 10.1% for `minor_findings`.

Where the journey goes quiet for them (`data/customer-journey.md`):
1. E-mail 3 "Your result is ready" carries no result, only a login link. 1,995 eligible customers never opened the report; they return at 2.2% vs 6.4% for openers.
2. The report is 4 pages, German only, "in medical language", and has **no** recommendation for when to come back.
3. After an unremarkable or minor result: "**no further contact** from Mirantus." Any follow-up depends on the optician; 3,192 eligible customers are at locations reporting `none` (4.1% return vs 8.3% for `phone`).

So the drop-off point is the report itself and the silence after it. No step in today's journey tells an unremarkable customer to come back, or reminds them.

## 3. Themes with two or more sources

**T1. "Unremarkable" is read as "done".**
- Customer, 67: "Warum? War doch alles in Ordnung."
- Ophthalmologist: "An unremarkable result is a snapshot, not a guarantee. Patients read it as 'I'm healthy'." and "It's the 'unremarkable' 60-year-olds who disappear."
- Cohort: unremarkable 3.5% vs minor_findings 10.1%, gap holds within every follow-up type, age band and report-opened group.

**T2. The report has no return interval, and the ophthalmologist would give one.**
- Journey: the report has "**no** recommendation for when to come back".
- Ophthalmologist: the form "has no field for a recommended interval. I would fill it in if it were there. It takes five seconds."
- S6: "Wenn im Befund steht 'Nächstes Screening in 12 Monaten', dann glauben die Leute das auch."

**T3. A trusted person's prompt brings people back.**
- Customer, 67: "Wenn Herr K. sagt, ich soll wieder kommen, dann komm ich wieder."
- Customer, 44: "Honestly I'd love a reminder. Just WhatsApp me in a year. I will forget otherwise."
- Cohort: optician `phone` follow-up 8.3% vs `none` 4.1%.

**T4. Consent given, nothing sent.**
- Customer, 44: ticked the reminders box; "Has received nothing since the report."
- Journey: no further contact after unremarkable/minor results.
- Cohort: consent true 6.0% vs false 3.7%. Share of consenting customers within `unremarkable`: not in the data (not cut in 01-cohort.md).

**T5. The report is hard to read, and language blocks opening.**
- Customer, 44: Google Translate, "half of it made no sense"; wants it "in English and in normal words".
- Customer, 67: "Da standen lauter Fachbegriffe drin."
- Ophthalmologist: "They are written for colleagues, honestly. Not for patients."
- Cohort: report open rate de 71.7% vs non-de 37.3%; among openers the language gap is 0.4 pp.

**T6. Opticians want customer contact under their own name.**
- Optician, Bavaria: "The customers are mine. If someone writes to them, it's me."
- S1 ("mit unserem Logo"), S4 ("Bitte keine Mails von Mirantus an meine Kunden"), S11 ("Der Befund sollte von uns kommen").
- Customer, 67: doesn't remember Mirantus; calls it "der Augen-Check bei Herrn K."

**T7. Opticians lack time and staff for manual follow-up.**
- Optician, Bavaria: "aber wer soll sich das merken?"; trained examiner left, screenings near zero for 6 weeks.
- S9 ("Wir haben keine Zeit, Kunden anzurufen. Es muss automatisch gehen."), S12 (lost trained person).

**T8. Price of a yearly repeat.**
- Customer, 67: "für einmal okay, aber jedes Jahr? Weiß ich nicht."
- S5: "69 € every year is a lot for pensioners."

**T9. E-mail is a weak channel for some customers.**
- Customer, 67: reads e-mail "ab und zu"; uses WhatsApp.
- Customer, 44: "Just WhatsApp me".
- S14: "SMS statt E-Mail. Unsere Kunden lesen keine E-Mails."
- Note: constraints name only "the report PDF and e-mails" as changeable. SMS/WhatsApp: not in the data.

**T10. Risk factors are not captured.**
- Customer, 67: sister has glaucoma; "nobody asked".
- Ophthalmologist: risk factors "aren't asked at the screening, so she often can't tell who should come back sooner."

## 4. Contradictions (kept, not merged)

- **Who the reminder should come from.** Customer, 44: "But not from the optician. I don't even remember which store it was. I'd want it from whoever has my results." vs. Customer, 67 (comes back if Herr K. says so), Optician, Bavaria, S1, S4, S11 (from the optician). Constraint: Mirantus may only contact "on the optician's behalf and with the optician's name on it".
- **Will opticians call?** S3 and Optician, Bavaria: "A list. Who should come back this month. Then my people can call." vs. S9 "Wir haben keine Zeit" and the same optician: "wer soll sich das merken?"
- **Do customers want to be reminded?** Customer, 44: "I'd love a reminder." vs. Optician, Bavaria: "Older customers find it pushy if you call them for something they didn't ask for." vs. Customer, 67 (the older customer): would come back if asked by her optician.
- **Is there a return problem at all?** S2: "Nothing, our customers come back for glasses anyway." vs. cohort: 5.0% eligible return rate. Optician, Bavaria, on her own data: "a few" came back, "can't say how many".
- **What the optician gets out of it.** S13: "Interessant ist es nur, wenn danach eine Brille verkauft wird." vs. Optician, Bavaria: it also "unterscheidet uns von der Kette nebenan."
- **Who decides.** S7: at chains, "HQ decides about customer communication, not the store." Other answers assume the store decides.

## 5. Candidate flows (at most two, not ranked)

Both target `unremarkable` customers and both depend on T2: the interval must come from the ophthalmologist's evaluation.

**Flow A — Interval in the report + optician-branded reminder e-mail.**
1. Ophthalmologist fills a new "next screening in N months" field on the evaluation form.
2. The report and the "Your result is ready" e-mail state that interval in plain words, with the optician's name.
3. Customers without consent are asked for it in that e-mail (a message they already receive legitimately).
4. At the due date, consenting customers get a reminder e-mail sent on the optician's behalf, with the optician's name, booking link to that store.
- Uses only changeable surfaces (report PDF, e-mails). No extra optician work.
- Open: chains may need HQ sign-off (S7); e-mail reach (T9); price (T8).

**Flow B — Interval in the report + "due this month" list for the optician.**
1. Same as A, steps 1–2.
2. The optician gets a monthly list of their consenting customers whose interval is due; their staff contact them.
- Matches S3 and the Bavaria optician's wish; phone follow-up has the highest return rate in step 1 (8.3%).
- Open: depends on staff time (S9, T7); cannot integrate into optician CRMs this quarter; whether a Mirantus optician dashboard exists today is not in the data.

# Constraints

Simplified for this case. Treat them as fixed.

## Consent (GDPR)

- Customers may only receive reminders or marketing if they gave `marketing_consent` at booking.

  legitimately, or in person.

## Medical advice

- mira is a non-medical screening. It is not a replacement for an eye examination by an
  ophthalmologist.
- Anything that sounds like a diagnosis or a treatment recommendation may only come from the
  evaluating ophthalmologist, in the report.
- Recommending a screening interval to a specific customer counts as a medical statement: it must
  come from the ophthalmologist's evaluation, not from marketing copy.
- No fear-based messaging ("you could go blind").

- By contract, the customer is the optician's customer. Mirantus may contact customers only for
  the service itself, or on the optician's behalf and with the optician's name on it.
- Opticians can't be required to do extra work, but they can be offered tools.

## Capacity

- One squad for one quarter: 2 engineers, 1 designer, you.
- The report PDF and e-mails can be changed. The opticians' own systems (their CRMs, cash
  registers) can't be integrated this quarter.

input.content:
# Decision memo: bring "unremarkable" customers back

Data is synthetic. Every number comes from `output/01-cohort.md`.

## The problem
Of the 5,773 customers who have had a full year to return, 287 came back: **5.0%**. The biggest leak is customers whose result was `unremarkable`. They are 3,995 customers (69%) and return at **3.5%**, against **10.1%** for `minor_findings`. That is 265 returns short, and the gap holds within every follow-up type, age band and report-opened group.

Today nothing tells them to come back. The report has no return interval, and after an unremarkable result there is "no further contact" (customer-journey.md). A customer, 67: "Warum? War doch alles in Ordnung." The ophthalmologist: "Patients read it as 'I'm healthy'."

## The decision
**Flow A: the ophthalmologist sets the interval, and the optician's name carries the reminder.**
- **Evaluation form:** a new "next screening in N months" field, filled in by the evaluating ophthalmologist. She "would fill it in if it were there."
- **Report and "Your result is ready" e-mail:** the interval in plain German, under the optician's name.
- **Consent re-ask:** in that same result e-mail, for customers who did not give `marketing_consent`. It is a message they already receive legitimately.
- **Reminder e-mail at the due date:** consenting customers only, sent on the optician's behalf with the optician's name, linking to booking at that store.
- **Opticians opt in.** No extra work for them. At chains, opt-in goes through HQ (survey answer S7).

## Ships in the next two weeks
The interval field, the report line, the result-e-mail copy with the consent re-ask, the reminder e-mail template, and the optician opt-in.

## Cut
- "Due this month" list for opticians (Flow B).
- SMS/WhatsApp. Constraints name only the PDF and e-mails as changeable.
- English or plain-language report.
- Second-screening discount.
- Risk-factor questions at the screening.
- Posters.
- Examiner training.

## Success metric
**Primary:** second-screening return rate for `unremarkable` customers in the eligible cohort (at least 12 months since first screening). The baseline is 3.5% and the comparator is 10.1%.

**Leading indicators**, which can be read early:
- consent opt-in from the result e-mail, among the 2,611 eligible customers without consent;
- bookings from the reminder e-mail;
- report open rate, with a baseline of 3,778 of 5,773 eligible customers.

## Guardrails
- No reminder goes to a customer without consent.
- No interval appears unless the ophthalmologist set it.
- No fear-based copy.
- Report open rate does not fall.
- Unsubscribes and optician opt-outs stay low. Threshold not in the data; set it before launch.
- The referral flow is untouched (`referral_booked` 4.9% vs 3.6% not booked).

## Test with real users inside two weeks
- **New screenings at opted-in opticians:** the ophthalmologist fills in the interval, and customers get the new report and result e-mail. Measure consent opt-in and report opens against the same opticians' prior customers. Call back a handful of customers to check that they understood the interval.
- **Back-catalogue:** take consenting `unremarkable` customers at opted-in opticians who are past 12 months and have not returned. Randomly split them into a reminder group and a holdout. The reminder states only the date of the last screening and the optician's name, with no interval and no medical claim. Measure bookings in each group within the two weeks.

**Decision rule:** ship to all opted-in opticians if reminder bookings beat the holdout and no guardrail breaks.

# Constraints

Simplified for this case. Treat them as fixed.

## Consent (GDPR)

- Customers may only receive reminders or marketing if they gave `marketing_consent` at booking.
- Without consent, the only messages allowed are those needed to deliver the service already
  bought (booking confirmation, appointment reminder, "your result is ready").
- Consent can be asked for again later, but only in a message the customer already receives
  legitimately, or in person.

## Medical advice

- mira is a non-medical screening. It is not a replacement for an eye examination by an
  ophthalmologist.
- Anything that sounds like a diagnosis or a treatment recommendation may only come from the
  evaluating ophthalmologist, in the report.
- Recommending a screening interval to a specific customer counts as a medical statement: it must
  come from the ophthalmologist's evaluation, not from marketing copy.
- No fear-based messaging ("you could go blind").

## The optician owns the relationship

- By contract, the customer is the optician's customer. Mirantus may contact customers only for
  the service itself, or on the optician's behalf and with the optician's name on it.
- Opticians can't be required to do extra work, but they can be offered tools.

## Capacity

- One squad for one quarter: 2 engineers, 1 designer, you.
- The report PDF and e-mails can be changed. The opticians' own systems (their CRMs, cash
  registers) can't be integrated this quarter.

# 04 — Prototype brief: Flow A

Input for the Design artifact in step 5. One flow only. Source: `output/03-decision-memo.md`. Rules are quoted from `data/constraints.md`, which I re-read before writing this copy.

## Goal of the prototype
Show one customer with an `unremarkable` result going from the ophthalmologist's evaluation to booking a second screening at the same optician. Test whether customers understand the interval and accept the reminder.

## Who and where
- **Customer:** first screening done; result `unremarkable`; customer-facing copy in German, because the report is German only today.
- **Ophthalmologist:** fills one new field.
- **Optician:** has opted in. Their name is on every customer-facing screen. No extra work for their staff.
- Placeholders: `[Optiker]` (store name), `[Ärztin]` (evaluating ophthalmologist), `[N]` (interval in months), `[Datum]`.

## Screens (one clickable path)

**1. Ophthalmologist evaluation form, new field**
- The existing form, plus a dropdown "Empfohlenes nächstes Screening": 12 / 24 / 36 Monate / keine Angabe. It is required before submitting.
- No default value. The interval must come from the ophthalmologist ("must come from the ophthalmologist's evaluation, not from marketing copy").

**2. E-mail "Ihr Ergebnis ist da"** (service message, so it is allowed without consent)
- Sender name: `[Optiker]` with mira.
- Subject: "Ihr Augen-Screening bei [Optiker]: Ihr Befund ist da"
- Body: "Ihr Befund von [Ärztin] liegt bereit. [Ärztin] empfiehlt Ihr nächstes Screening in [N] Monaten."
- Button: "Befund ansehen"
- **Consent re-ask.** Shown only if `marketing_consent` = false. The checkbox is unticked: "☐ Ja, [Optiker] darf mich per E-Mail erinnern, wenn mein nächstes Screening fällig ist." Below it: "Sie können das jederzeit abbestellen."
- The e-mail contains no result itself.

**3. Report, page 1, new box at the top**
- "Nächstes Screening: in [N] Monaten, empfohlen von [Ärztin]."
- "Ein unauffälliger Befund zeigt den heutigen Stand. Ein regelmäßiges Screening hilft, Veränderungen früh zu sehen."
- Footer line: "mira ist ein nicht-medizinisches Screening und ersetzt keine augenärztliche Untersuchung."
- The rest of the report stays as it is.

**4. Reminder e-mail at the due date** (consenting customers only)
- Sender name: `[Optiker]`.
- Subject: "Ihr nächstes Augen-Screening bei [Optiker]"
- Body: "Am [Datum] waren Sie bei uns zum Augen-Screening. [Ärztin] hat damals empfohlen, nach [N] Monaten wiederzukommen. Dieser Zeitpunkt ist jetzt."
- Button: "Termin bei [Optiker] buchen"
- Footer: unsubscribe link.
- *Copy variant for the back-catalogue test only* (same screen, no interval exists for these customers): "Am [Datum] waren Sie bei uns zum Augen-Screening. Möchten Sie einen neuen Termin vereinbaren?" No interval and no medical claim.

**5. Booking page**
- Pre-set to `[Optiker]`'s location, showing free slots. Confirm. This is followed by the existing booking confirmation e-mail.

## Copy rules (from `data/constraints.md`)
- "No fear-based messaging ("you could go blind")." No words like Risiko, Erblindung, Gefahr.
- The interval appears only where `[Ärztin]` set it, and always attributed to her.
- No diagnosis or treatment language outside the report.
- No reminder without consent: screen 4 is unreachable in the prototype when consent = false.
- The optician's name is on screens 2, 4 and 5 ("on the optician's behalf and with the optician's name on it").

## Out of scope
Flow B (due list), SMS/WhatsApp, translations, discounts, risk-factor questions, and any second flow.

## What to observe with test customers
- After screen 3, can they say when to come back, and who said so?
- On screen 2, do they tick the consent box, and why or why not?
- On screen 4, does the sender feel familiar? Does it feel pushy? (The optician interview says older customers may find it pushy. Keep this contradiction open.)

The href is the target's path relative to this artboard's; a leading `/` means the canvas root (`/sub/Cart.dc.html`). Style the `<a>` itself as the button: a `<button>` or input inside it swallows the click. `href="#id"` scrolls within the artboard; `https://…` opens a tab. Each artboard keeps its own `state`, so a flow that must share state across screens is ONE artboard: its handlers set a `state` field, `renderVals()` returns one flag per screen from it, and each screen sits in its own `<sc-if>`. - **Conditional styling in a loop**: precompute the varying piece per item in `renderVals()` (e.g. each item carries `ringStyle` or `selected`) and either branch with `<sc-if>` or bind the computed value — a style hole is acceptable for live, state-driven values (selection highlights) and for a declared tweak prop (`{{accent}}`), just never for other static theme tokens, which belong inline so they paint while streaming. - **Logic class**: plain classic JS, no TypeScript, no import/export; must be `class Component extends DCLogic`. You get `this.props`, `state`/`setState`/`forceUpdate` and React class lifecycle (`componentDidMount`…), minus `render()`. `renderVals()` returns the template's inputs: flat values, arrays, handlers, refs. - **`data-props` editors** (on the `<script type="text/x-dc" data-dc-script>` tag): per-prop `{"editor": "text"|"color"|"int"|"float"|"range"|"boolean"| "enum"|null, "default": …, "tsType": "…"}` plus `options` for enum, `min`/`max`/`step`/`unit` for numbers/range, `section` to group; on color, `options` as a 3–4-item list of hex strings renders swatches. `editor: null` for callbacks/objects. Editable props open in the panel's Tweaks tab from the artboard's Tweaks button (which props deserve an editor: below). `default` seeds the editor only — fall back with `this.props.x ?? …` in `renderVals()`. `$preview: {"width", "height"}` sets the preferred preview size for sized fragments (a PAGE declares it too: its frame's `w`×`h`). - **Tweaks are levers, not copy.** Every `data-props` entry with an editor becomes a control in the Tweaks tab, so declare few, deliberate ones: behavioral switches (a dark or density toggle, a variant enum, an item count) and values that cut across the design in many places (one accent or tint color, a spacing or type scale). Do NOT make tweaks for label or body copy unless the user asks — write copy as literal text in the markup (not a prop, and not a `renderVals()` binding unless it is genuinely data) so viewers retype it in place in the WYSIWYG editor — and do not make a tweak for a color used in a single place; they restyle that element in the properties panel. - **`data-props` escaping**: it is a normal HTML attribute — the runtime reads it with `getAttribute` and then JSON-parses, so HTML entities decode first: write `&` for `&`, `'` for a literal single quote, and JSON `\"` for double quotes inside strings. Single-quote the attribute itself (`data-props='…'`) — every example assumes it, and a double-quoted attribute changes which characters need escaping. Those three escapes are the complete list: raw UTF-8 (em-dashes, middle dots, accented letters) is safe as-is, no numeric entities needed. - **Editable text, including multi-line**: a `{{hole}}` bound to a `data-props` entry with `{"editor": "text"}` renders as a TEXT node — HTML in the value is escaped, so `<br>` will not work. For multi-line text, pair `\n` in the JSON default with `white-space: pre-line` (or `pre-wrap`) in the bound element's inline style — without it HTML collapses the newline to a space and the lines run together (a real shipped bug: a two-line band lineup rendered as one merged line). For rich per-line layout, split into multiple props, one element each. - **Child DCs**: `<dc-import name="Card" item="{{ it }}" hint-size="100%,120px"></dc-import>` mounts the sibling file `Card.dc.html` (which is also an artboard of its own); every other attribute becomes a prop on the child (kebab→camel, read as `this.props.item` — declare it in the child's `data-props` with `"editor": null` when it is an object or callback; avoid a prop named `name`, which selects the component); `hint-size="W,H"` (CSS lengths) is the placeholder box shown until the child renders, so match the child's root size; works inside `<sc-for>`; never self-close and never use capitalized tags (`<Card/>`).

Step 5 is done, so the workflow is complete. The prototype is here: https://claude.ai/artifact/BZ72zi9K348i7ZeeAiVru6, and the link is saved in [05-prototype.md](output/05-prototype.md). I haven't clicked through it or rendered it myself.

It's one flow in five screens, in German, with names, dates and addresses as placeholders in [brackets]:
1. **Ophthalmologist's form:** a new required field for when the next screening is due. Nothing is pre-selected.
2. **"Ihr Ergebnis ist da" e-mail:** sent under the optician's name and states the recommended interval. Customers who didn't consent at booking also see a consent checkbox, unticked by default.
3. **Report:** a box at the top with the interval and who recommended it, plus the line saying mira is not a medical examination.
4. **Reminder e-mail at the due date:** from the optician, with an unsubscribe link.
5. **Booking:** a time slot at the same optician.

A switch at the top sets whether the customer consented at booking. If the customer has no consent and leaves the checkbox unticked, or the ophthalmologist picks "keine Angabe", the flow ends after the report and no reminder appears.

The brief also had a reminder variant for customers screened before the change, which the memo's two-week test uses. I didn't build it as a screen.

The canvas is private. Anyone else needs you to share it from the page's Share menu before they can open it.
